regime.label: Leaning Bullish
summary: Cycle: Late-Cycle Overheat — growth rising, inflation rising (confidence high).
Liquidity is roughly neutral — expect ROTATION rather than big net inflows.
Strongest positives: Yield curve normal (+0.38%); Unemployment 4.2% (-0.1 pp 6M); Sahm rule 0.00 (trigger 0.50).
Biggest risks: Fed is hiking (+24 bp in 6M); Bond market expects rate hikes; Real yield 2.63%.

phase.label: Late-Cycle Overheat
phase.description: Growth is strong but inflation is heating up and the Fed leans hawkish. Real assets — commodities, energy, materials — historically lead; long bonds suffer.

moneyFlow.headline: Liquidity is roughly neutral — expect ROTATION rather than big net inflows
moneyFlow.detail: Without a strong liquidity push either way, money tends to move between sectors and styles. Follow relative strength (sector rotation map below).

metrics.name: Net Liquidity (Fed − TGA − Reverse Repo)
metrics.headline: Net liquidity falling (-1.4% in 3M)
metrics.what: The dollars actually available to financial markets: the Fed's balance sheet minus cash parked in the Treasury's account (TGA) and the Fed's reverse-repo facility. Historically one of the tightest macro correlates of stock prices.
metrics.now: Liquidity is roughly flat (-1.4% over 3 months).
metrics.next: Neutral liquidity means returns depend more on earnings and rotation than on new money.

metrics.name: Fed Balance Sheet ("Money Printing")
metrics.headline: Fed balance sheet flat (+0.1% 3M)
metrics.what: Total assets held by the Federal Reserve. When it grows (QE) the Fed is creating money to buy bonds; when it shrinks (QT) it is pulling money out of the system.
metrics.now: The balance sheet is roughly stable — QT has slowed or stopped, neither adding nor draining much.
metrics.next: A flat balance sheet removes a headwind; a pivot to expansion would be a strong bullish trigger.

metrics.name: M2 Money Supply Growth (YoY)
metrics.headline: M2 growing 5.7% a year
metrics.what: All cash, checking, savings and money-market balances in the economy. Its growth rate shows whether there is more or less money circulating.
metrics.now: Money supply is growing at a normal pace (5.7%/yr, long-run average ~6%).
metrics.next: Growth rate is stable — no major change in the money backdrop.

metrics.name: Fed Reverse Repo (Idle Cash Buffer)
metrics.headline: Reverse repo at $4B
metrics.what: Cash money-market funds park at the Fed overnight. When it falls, that idle cash moves into T-bills and markets — offsetting QT.
metrics.now: This buffer is nearly empty. Any further QT or Treasury cash-building now drains bank reserves directly.
metrics.next: With the cushion gone, funding-market stress (repo spikes) becomes more likely if liquidity keeps tightening — a reason for the Fed to stop QT.

metrics.name: Treasury Cash Account (TGA)
metrics.headline: Treasury cash up $89B in 3M
metrics.what: The US government's checking account at the Fed. When the Treasury builds it up (by issuing debt) it pulls cash out of markets; when it spends it down, cash flows back.
metrics.now: Treasury cash balance is fairly stable.
metrics.next: Debt-ceiling fights and big tax dates swing this account by hundreds of billions — watch it around those events.

metrics.name: Fed Funds Rate
metrics.headline: Fed is hiking (+24 bp in 6M)
metrics.what: The overnight interest rate the Fed controls. It sets the cost of money for the entire economy.
metrics.now: The Fed is raising rates — money is getting more expensive.
metrics.next: Hikes usually pressure valuations, small caps and real estate.

metrics.name: Market-Implied Fed Path (2Y − Fed Funds)
metrics.headline: Bond market expects rate hikes
metrics.what: The 2-year Treasury yield minus the Fed funds rate. The 2-year tracks where traders expect the Fed to be over the next two years.
metrics.now: The 2-year sits 73 bp above the Fed rate — traders expect hikes.
metrics.next: If the Fed under-delivers versus these expectations, markets typically wobble; over-delivering is a tailwind.

metrics.name: 10-Year Treasury Yield
metrics.headline: 10Y yield 4.98% (+30 bp 3M)
metrics.what: The benchmark long-term interest rate. It drives mortgage rates and the discount rate used to value every stock.
metrics.now: Long rates are relatively stable.
metrics.next: A sustained break above 5% would favor cash and value over growth; a drop below 4% would favor long bonds, tech and real estate.

metrics.name: 10-Year Real Yield (after inflation)
metrics.headline: Real yield 2.63%
metrics.what: The inflation-adjusted return on safe government bonds (TIPS). High real yields make cash and bonds attractive versus stocks, gold and crypto.
metrics.now: Real yields are restrictive (>2%): safe bonds pay well, raising the bar for risky assets.
metrics.next: Falling real yields have historically been one of the strongest tailwinds for gold and long-duration tech.

metrics.name: Yield Curve (10Y − 2Y)
metrics.headline: Yield curve normal (+0.38%)
metrics.what: Long-term minus short-term rates. Normally positive. When it inverts (negative), it has preceded every US recession since the 1960s — usually by 6-24 months.
metrics.now: The curve has a normal positive slope — consistent with expansion.
metrics.next: A steepening curve favors banks (Financials) and cyclicals.

metrics.name: Yield Curve (10Y − 3M)
metrics.headline: Yield curve recently un-inverted (+0.78%)
metrics.what: Long-term minus short-term rates. Normally positive. When it inverts (negative), it has preceded every US recession since the 1960s — usually by 6-24 months.
metrics.now: The curve has just turned positive after an inversion. Historically recessions often START around this point — stay alert.
metrics.next: Watch jobless claims and the Sahm rule for confirmation of a slowdown.

metrics.name: CPI Inflation (YoY)
metrics.headline: CPI Inflation 3.7% and rising
metrics.what: How fast consumer prices are rising versus a year ago.
metrics.now: Running at 3.7% vs the Fed's 2% target, and re-accelerating over the last 3 months.
metrics.next: Re-accelerating inflation limits Fed cuts and favors commodities, energy and TIPS over long bonds.

metrics.name: Core CPI (ex Food & Energy, YoY)
metrics.headline: Core CPI 2.6% and flat
metrics.what: Inflation excluding volatile food and energy — the "sticky" trend the Fed watches most closely.
metrics.now: Running at 2.6% vs the Fed's 2% target, and roughly stable over the last 3 months.
metrics.next: Stable inflation keeps the Fed on its current path.

metrics.name: 5-Year Inflation Expectations (Market)
metrics.headline: Markets expect 2.46% inflation
metrics.what: The inflation rate bond traders are pricing in over the next 5 years (nominal minus inflation-protected Treasury yield).
metrics.now: Expectations are reasonably anchored near the Fed's target.
metrics.next: Rising expectations favor gold, commodities and energy; falling expectations favor long-term bonds.

metrics.name: Unemployment Rate
metrics.headline: Unemployment 4.2% (-0.1 pp 6M)
metrics.what: Share of the labor force without a job. The direction matters more than the level.
metrics.now: Unemployment is stable or falling — the job market is healthy.
metrics.next: A rise of 0.5 pp from the low (the Sahm rule) has reliably marked the start of recessions.

metrics.name: Sahm Rule Recession Indicator
metrics.headline: Sahm rule 0.00 (trigger 0.50)
metrics.what: Compares the 3-month average unemployment rate to its 12-month low. A reading of 0.50+ has signalled every US recession since 1970 in real time.
metrics.now: Far from the recession trigger.
metrics.next: No recession signal from jobs data.

metrics.name: Initial Jobless Claims (4-wk avg)
metrics.headline: Jobless claims 197K (-5.3% vs 6M avg)
metrics.what: New unemployment-benefit filings each week — the most timely read on layoffs.
metrics.now: Layoffs are low and falling.
metrics.next: A sustained rise above ~300K has historically coincided with recessions.

metrics.name: Atlanta Fed GDPNow (real GDP, annualized)
metrics.headline: GDP tracking 3.2%
metrics.what: A real-time model estimate of current-quarter economic growth.
metrics.now: The economy is growing above trend.
metrics.next: Above-trend growth supports earnings and cyclical sectors; sub-1% growth raises recession odds.

metrics.name: Consumer Sentiment (U. Michigan)
metrics.headline: Consumer sentiment 48.1
metrics.what: How optimistic households feel. Long-run average is ~85.
metrics.now: Consumers are deeply pessimistic — near historic lows.
metrics.next: Contrarian signal: extreme gloom has historically been followed by above-average 12-month stock returns — but it weighs on spending.

metrics.name: High-Yield Credit Spread
metrics.headline: Junk-bond spreads 3.26%
metrics.what: Extra yield investors demand to lend to risky companies. "Smart money" in credit markets often spots trouble before stock investors do.
metrics.now: Spreads are tight — lenders are relaxed (supportive, though it can signal complacency).
metrics.next: A fast widening (+100 bp) has preceded most major stock drawdowns — the key early-warning to watch.

metrics.name: Financial Conditions (Chicago Fed NFCI)
metrics.headline: Financial conditions loose (-0.49)
metrics.what: A composite of 105 measures of credit, leverage and risk. Negative = easier than average, positive = tighter.
metrics.now: Money is easy to get — conditions are loose.
metrics.next: Loose conditions fuel risk-taking; a move above 0 has historically accompanied bear markets.

metrics.name: VIX "Fear Index"
metrics.headline: VIX 17.2
metrics.what: Expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, from options prices.
metrics.now: Normal, slightly cautious.
metrics.next: No extreme reading.

metrics.name: US Dollar (Trade-Weighted)
metrics.headline: Dollar stronger (+0.5% 3M)
metrics.what: The dollar versus major trading partners. A rising dollar tightens global liquidity because much of the world borrows in dollars.
metrics.now: The dollar is range-bound.
metrics.next: A weaker dollar historically favors emerging markets, commodities, gold and multinational earnings.

metrics.name: S&P 500 vs 200-Day Average
metrics.headline: S&P 500 above its 200-day trend (+4.1%)
metrics.what: How far the S&P 500 is from its 200-day moving average — the line professionals use to define bull vs bear trends.
metrics.now: The primary trend is up (bull market).
metrics.next: A close below ~$726 on SPY would flip the trend to bearish.

metrics.name: S&P 500 Distance from 52-Week High
metrics.headline: S&P 500 -3.0% below its high
metrics.what: How far the market has fallen from its highest close over the past year.
metrics.now: Near highs — buyers are in control.
metrics.next: No sign of a major breakdown yet.

metrics.name: Market Breadth (% of sectors above 200-day)
metrics.headline: 8/11 sectors in uptrends
metrics.what: How many of the 11 S&P sectors are trading above their own 200-day average. Healthy bull markets are broad; narrow rallies led by a few sectors are fragile.
metrics.now: Participation is broad — a healthy market.
metrics.next: Watch for divergences: index at highs while breadth falls has often preceded corrections.

metrics.name: Discretionary vs Staples (XLY/XLP)
metrics.headline: Discretionary vs Staples falling (-5.9% 3M)
metrics.what: Wants vs needs. When investors buy consumer discretionary over staples they are betting on a strong consumer.
metrics.now: Money is hiding in staples — a defensive signal.
metrics.next: Defensive rotation underway — favors quality and safety.

metrics.name: Junk Bonds vs Treasuries (HYG/IEF)
metrics.headline: Junk Bonds vs Treasuries falling (-0.9% 3M)
metrics.what: Credit risk appetite. Bond investors (often the smartest money) choosing junk over Treasuries = confidence.
metrics.now: Flat — no strong signal either way.
metrics.next: Watch for a break in either direction.

metrics.name: Copper / Gold Ratio (×1000)
metrics.headline: Copper / Gold Ratio rising (+5.7% 3M)
metrics.what: Copper is an industrial metal (growth); gold is a safe haven (fear). Their ratio is a classic real-time growth gauge that also tracks bond yields.
metrics.now: Growth expectations are improving.
metrics.next: Risk appetite confirmed — favors cyclical, higher-beta exposure.

metrics.name: Small Caps vs Large Caps (IWM/SPY)
metrics.headline: Small Caps vs Large Caps falling (-5.2% 3M)
metrics.what: Small companies depend on cheap credit and a strong domestic economy. Leadership by small caps signals broadening, liquidity-driven risk appetite.
metrics.now: Money prefers the safety of mega-caps — narrow, defensive leadership.
metrics.next: Defensive rotation underway — favors quality and safety.

metrics.name: Geopolitical Headline Risk (0-100)
metrics.headline: Headline risk 63/100 (elevated)
metrics.what: Share of negative vs positive headlines across wars/geopolitics, trade/tariffs and energy news over the last 2-3 days (keyword-based tone). 50 = balanced.
metrics.now: News flow is dominated by conflict, tariffs or energy shocks.
metrics.next: Geopolitical shocks usually cause short, sharp sell-offs; they only change the trend when they hit oil prices, inflation or credit. This history builds one point per day.

scenarios.name: Bull case — money keeps flowing in
scenarios.narrative: Liquidity stays supportive, inflation behaves and the Fed eases without a recession. Breadth widens beyond the leaders, small caps and cyclicals catch up. Leaders today: Energy, Materials, Crude Oil.
triggers: Net liquidity rising for another quarter

scenarios.name: Base case — Overheat playbook with rotation
scenarios.narrative: The economy stays in Late-Cycle Overheat. Index returns are moderate and driven by sector rotation: Growth is strong but inflation is heating up and the Fed leans hawkish. Real assets — commodities, energy, materials — historically lead; long bonds suffer.
triggers: Fed follows the path the 2-year yield is pricing

scenarios.name: Bear case — money leaves risk assets
scenarios.narrative: A growth scare, inflation flare-up or shock (geopolitical, credit or policy) drains risk appetite. Cash, Treasuries, gold and defensives outperform. Current warning lights: Fed is hiking (+24 bp in 6M); Bond market expects rate hikes; Real yield 2.63%.

watch.note: A close below flips the trend to bearish.

copperGold.name: Dr. Copper / Gold Ratio
copperGold.summary: Dr. Copper is outperforming Gold (+5.7% 3M), signaling real-world physical demand and manufacturing acceleration.
copperGold.interpretation: When industrial copper beats safety gold, global economic growth is expanding rather than contracting.
copperGold.advice: 🟢 TRADING ADVICE: Overweight Industrials (XLI), Materials (XLB), and Small Caps (IWM). Keep bond duration short.

buffettIndicator.name: The Buffett Indicator (Market Cap to GDP)
buffettIndicator.summary: Total US stock market capitalization sits at 194.5% of GDP, well above the historical fair value baseline of 115%.
buffettIndicator.interpretation: Long-term broad market valuation is stretched; projected 10-year broad index compound returns are lower than historical averages.
buffettIndicator.advice: 🟡 TRADING ADVICE: Avoid buying broad index funds blindly at all-time highs; focus on cheap cash-flow value stocks and keep 20% in 5% cash.

putCallSentiment.name: Put-to-Call & Options Sentiment
putCallSentiment.summary: Put-to-Call ratio sits at 0.84 with overall market sentiment at 58/100, showing steady investor confidence without extreme panic or mania.
putCallSentiment.interpretation: Options traders are moderately optimistic; there is neither peak euphoria to cause an immediate crash nor extreme panic to buy a capitulation bottom.
putCallSentiment.advice: 🟢 TRADING ADVICE: Ride current winners with trailing stop-losses; wait for Put-to-Call spikes above 1.10 before aggressively adding new leverage.

dollarTrend.name: U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) Trend
dollarTrend.summary: The US Dollar is trading in a stable range around 104.3, removing the global liquidity squeeze caused by previous rapid dollar spikes.
dollarTrend.interpretation: A stable or softening Dollar acts as a tailwind for raw commodities, precious metals, and emerging market equities.
dollarTrend.advice: 🟢 TRADING ADVICE: Dollar stability is green light for Gold (GLD), Crude Oil (USO), and Emerging Markets (EEM). Avoid holding unhedged foreign cash.

insiderRatio.name: Corporate Insider Buy/Sell Ratio
insiderRatio.summary: Corporate executives are selectively buying their own shares (0.32 ratio), with heavy cluster-buying concentrated in Energy and Financials.
insiderRatio.interpretation: Insiders with real-time access to customer order books are putting their own personal wealth into cyclical value companies.
insiderRatio.advice: 🟢 TRADING ADVICE: Follow executive insider cluster purchases in Energy (XLE) and Regional Banks; avoid tech names with heavy insider dumping.

yieldCurveUninversion.name: Yield Curve 10Y-2Y Spread & Un-Inversion
yieldCurveUninversion.summary: The 10Y-2Y Treasury yield curve has un-inverted to +0.38% after being inverted for over two years.
yieldCurveUninversion.interpretation: The un-inversion steepens the curve, which boosts bank net interest margins (Financials XLF), but historically starts the 6-18 month recession countdown clock.
yieldCurveUninversion.advice: 🟢 TRADING ADVICE: Buy Financials (XLF) for steepening curve margins; maintain strict stops and watch unemployment claims for recession confirmation.
